My point estimates were anchored primarily to what appears to be a current price level around $360–363, with modest upward drift built in across horizons. For the one-day estimate, I leaned on short-term mean reversion and the assumption that prices rarely make dramatic moves in a single session absent a major catalyst, so $362.5 reflects little more than continuity from the prevailing level. For the one-week estimate, I added a small positive drift of roughly $1.50, consistent with a mild bullish bias that often shows up in broad equity indices or similar instruments over multi-day windows when no clear headwinds are apparent. The one-month estimate extended that drift slightly further to $367, reflecting a longer compounding of modest expected returns while acknowledging that over four weeks, mean reversion forces and trend continuation can both play meaningful roles.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each time horizon. For one day, the $21 range (352 to 373) corresponds to roughly a 1–1.5% daily move on either side, which is consistent with normal market conditions. As the horizon extended to one week, I widened the band to $40, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty and the greater chance of an accumulating sequence of adverse or favorable sessions. The one-month interval of $85 (325 to 410) accounts for the substantially higher variance over that window, including the possibility of regime shifts, earnings-related moves, or macroeconomic surprises that are unlikely in a single day but plausible over a month.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a surprise inflation reading, an aggressive central bank statement, or a geopolitical shock — could drive prices well below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. A liquidity event or credit stress episode could amplify moves sharply. On the upside, an unexpected dovish pivot from a major central bank, a blowout economic report, or a resolution of a geopolitical flashpoint could send prices surging past the upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where tail events have more time to materialize.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals implicitly assume a relatively stable volatility environment. If realized volatility spikes — as it sometimes does during earnings seasons, Federal Reserve meetings, or geopolitical flare-ups — the true distribution of outcomes would have much fatter tails than my stated intervals capture. Conversely, in an unusually calm, low-volume environment, the actual range of outcomes could be considerably narrower than my one-week and one-month intervals suggest.
